market_context: United States/general English; comparison of heme iron in organ meats and muscle cuts
title: Meats highest in iron

seo.title: Meats highest in iron: liver, beef, lamb and poultry
seo.meta_description: Liver stands out: 3 oz cooked beef liver provides ~5 mg iron, versus ~2 mg in many beef cuts and about 1 mg in chicken or turkey.
seo.search_intent: Compare meats by iron content and understand why organ meats provide much more than ordinary muscle cuts.

excerpt: If organ meats are included, liver wins by a wide margin. NIH lists about 5 mg iron in 3 oz (85 g) cooked beef liver, versus ~2 mg in 85 g lean beef round and about 1 mg in similar servings of chicken or turkey. Much of meat iron is also highly bioavailable heme iron.
content_html:
Rankings of iron-rich meat look very different depending on whether organ meats are included. Liver contains substantially more iron than most ordinary muscle cuts.

Comparable serving sizes

FoodServingApprox. iron
Beef liver, cooked3 oz / 85 g~5 mg
Beef bottom round, braised and trimmed3 oz / 85 g~2 mg
Cooked leg of lamb3 oz / 85 g~2 mg
Roasted chicken3 oz / 85 g~1 mg
Roasted turkey3 oz / 85 g~1 mg

That makes a serving of liver roughly 2.5 times the iron in a comparable lean-beef serving and about five times the amount in chicken or turkey in these references.

The pattern is similar per 100 g

Five milligrams per 85 g liver works out to roughly 5.9 mg/100 g. Two milligrams in lean beef is about 2.4 mg/100 g, while 1 mg per 85 g poultry is roughly 1.2 mg/100 g.

Meat iron has an absorption advantage

Meat provides both heme and nonheme iron. Heme iron is generally absorbed more efficiently and is less affected by meal inhibitors than plant nonheme iron, so milligrams alone do not tell the full story.

More iron does not mean liver every day

Liver is highly concentrated not only in iron but also in vitamin A and other micronutrients. Because it is so nutrient-dense, it does not need to be eaten daily to make a substantial contribution.

Red meat generally beats poultry

Among ordinary muscle cuts, beef and lamb typically provide more iron than chicken or turkey breast. Exact numbers still vary with the cut, animal and cooking method.

The practical takeaway

If organ meats count, liver is clearly the iron leader. Among common muscle meats, beef and lamb generally rank above chicken and turkey but far below liver.

faq.question: Which meat has the most iron?
faq.answer: If organ meats are included, liver stands out. NIH lists about 5 mg iron in 3 oz cooked beef liver.

faq.question: Does beef have more iron than chicken?
faq.answer: In comparable references, yes: about 2 mg per 3 oz lean beef versus roughly 1 mg per 3 oz roasted chicken.

faq.question: Is meat iron well absorbed?
faq.answer: Yes. Some is heme iron, which generally has higher bioavailability than plant nonheme iron.
